package_info.package_name: Weaponized LNK Initial Access Chain (Blank Grabber, Redline Stealer, NetSupport RAT)
package_info.package_manager: Windows OS (malicious LNK, HTA, VBScript, PowerShell payloads)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire package is malicious because it orchestrates a multi-stage attack chain leveraging weaponized LNK files to execute remote scripts and download infostealers and RATs, resulting in credential theft, data exfiltration, and unauthorized remote access. The chain abuses trusted Windows utilities (cmstp.exe, PowerShell) for payload delivery, UAC bypass, and persistence, with no legitimate use in this context.

execution_context.trigger: User interaction (double-clicking or opening the malicious LNK file)
execution_context.file_location: Malicious LNK file (e.g., disguised as PDF in ZIP/ISO attachment, typically in Downloads or email attachment directory)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: LNK file command: cmstp.exe /s /au <remote .inf or .hta profile>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the LNK file, the code launches cmstp.exe with a remote profile, which initiates the download and execution of a remote .hta file, resulting in arbitrary code execution on the system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: LNK files are not expected to launch system utilities like cmstp.exe with remote profiles, especially from user directories or email attachments. This behavior is a known technique for initial access and code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal LNK files should point to local applications or documents, not execute system utilities with remote scripts or profiles.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IT administrators may use cmstp.exe for legitimate VPN or network profile deployment, but never via LNK files delivered through email attachments or disguised as documents.
key_indicators: LNK file disguised as a PDF or document
cmstp.exe invoked with a remote resource as argument
LNK file delivered via email or messaging platforms
Execution of cmstp.exe from user-accessible directories

execution_context.trigger: Execution of cmstp.exe (triggered by LNK file)
execution_context.file_location: Remote .hta file (e.g., hxxp://94.156.253[.]17/Downloads/careabout[.]hta, loaded over the network)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: <script language='VBScript'> ... Download and execute obfuscated VBScript ... </script>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon execution by cmstp.exe, the remote .hta file runs embedded VBScript that downloads an obfuscated VBScript payload from a remote server and executes it, enabling further code execution and establishing a foothold.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: HTA files loaded from remote sources via cmstp.exe are highly unusual and are a known vector for code execution and malware delivery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Connection Manager profiles should not contain or execute scripts that download and run additional code, especially from untrusted remote sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: HTA files may be used for legitimate automation in enterprise environments, but not in the context of remote profiles delivered via email or user directories.
key_indicators: HTA file delivered and executed via cmstp.exe
VBScript within HTA downloads further payloads
Obfuscated script content in HTA
Remote HTA file hosted on suspicious or non-corporate domains

execution_context.file_location: Downloaded VBScript (retrieved from remote server, executed in memory)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
Set objShell = CreateObject("Wscript.Shell")
objShell.Run "powershell -w hidden -nop -c <obfuscated PowerShell loader>"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the downloaded VBScript executes, it de-obfuscates and launches a PowerShell loader in hidden and no-profile mode, which then downloads and executes the next stage malware, continuing the attack chain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: VBScript launching PowerShell in hidden/no-profile mode is a common malware technique to evade user detection and security controls.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts rarely launch PowerShell in this manner, especially as part of a chain initiated from email-delivered files or remote HTA scripts.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System administrators may automate tasks with VBScript and PowerShell, but not through this obfuscated, multi-stage delivery chain.
key_indicators: Obfuscated PowerShell command embedded in VBScript
PowerShell launched with -w hidden and -nop flags
Chained execution from HTA to VBScript to PowerShell
VBScript retrieved from remote, non-corporate servers

execution_context.trigger: Execution of PowerShell loader (launched by VBScript)
execution_context.file_location: PowerShell loader (executed in memory, invoked by VBScript)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the PowerShell loader runs, it downloads a PDF and an EXE (Redline Stealer) to the AppData\Roaming directory, then uses cmstp.exe with specific arguments to bypass UAC and execute the downloaded EXE, escalating privileges and enabling malware execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: PowerShell scripts that download executables from untrusted sources and invoke cmstp.exe for UAC bypass are strongly indicative of malware delivery and privilege escalation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate PowerShell scripts should not download and execute files from suspicious domains, nor perform UAC bypass using system utilities in this manner.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may download files, but not with obfuscated chains, from untrusted sources, or using UAC bypass techniques.
key_indicators: Invoke-WebRequest to suspicious or non-corporate domains
Files dropped in AppData\Roaming with non-standard names
cmstp.exe used for UAC bypass and execution of downloaded EXE
PowerShell process tree originating from script or HTA

execution_context.trigger: Execution of EXE (Redline Stealer, launched by PowerShell post-UAC bypass)
execution_context.file_location: AppData\Roaming\71iqujprzsp4w.exe (Redline Stealer binary, dropped by PowerShell)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the Redline Stealer executable runs, it collects credentials, browser data, and other sensitive information from the system, then exfiltrates this data to attacker-controlled servers, establishing persistence and enabling further compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Redline Stealer is a well-known infostealer malware family, and its presence on any system is always malicious due to its credential harvesting and exfiltration capabilities.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate software should collect and exfiltrate credentials, browser data, or other sensitive information to external servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There are no legitimate uses for Redline Stealer or similar infostealer binaries.
key_indicators: Credential harvesting from browsers and system stores
Network exfiltration to attacker-controlled infrastructure
Persistence mechanisms to maintain access
Execution of known infostealer binary in user profile directories

attack_chain.action: User opens malicious LNK file, which launches cmstp.exe with a remote profile.
cmstp.exe executes a remote .hta file containing obfuscated VBScript.
VBScript de-obfuscates and launches a PowerShell loader in hidden mode.
PowerShell downloads malware files (PDF and EXE) to AppData\Roaming and uses cmstp.exe for UAC bypass.
Redline Stealer executes, harvesting and exfiltrating sensitive data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data exfiltration and potential further compromise

behavioral_signatures: LNK file execution launching cmstp.exe with remote profile as argument
cmstp.exe executing remote .hta files from non-corporate or suspicious domains
HTA or VBScript launching PowerShell with -w hidden and -nop flags
PowerShell processes downloading executables to AppData\Roaming
cmstp.exe invoked by PowerShell for UAC bypass and execution of dropped EXE
Execution of known infostealer binaries (Redline Stealer, Blank Grabber, NetSupport RAT) in user profile directories
Chained process tree: LNK → cmstp.exe → HTA → VBScript → PowerShell → cmstp.exe → infostealer EXE
file_indicators: LNK files disguised as PDFs or documents in email attachments or downloads
Files dropped in %APPDATA%\Roaming with suspicious or random names (e.g., Inv.pdf, 71iqujprzsp4w.exe)
Presence of HTA files loaded from remote, non-corporate sources
Redline Stealer or similar infostealer binaries present in user profile directories
network_indicators: Connections to a0840501.xsph[.]ru, transfer.sh, onlythefamily[.]ddns.net, montec-shop[.]de, 94.156.253[.]17
Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to uncommon TLDs or dynamic DNS domains
Exfiltration of data to attacker-controlled servers identified in the report
Network traffic to IPs and domains associated with infostealer C2 infrastructure
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for LNK file executions that invoke cmstp.exe with remote profiles, especially from user directories or email attachment locations. Detect and block HTA file execution from remote sources. Alert on PowerShell processes launched by scripts or HTA files, particularly those that download files to AppData\Roaming or invoke cmstp.exe for UAC bypass. Flag the presence and execution of known infostealer binaries (e.g., Redline Stealer) in user profile directories. Correlate process trees that match the described attack chain. Monitor for network connections to the listed suspicious domains and IPs, and block or alert on exfiltration attempts to these endpoints. Use file and network IOCs in conjunction with behavioral signatures for comprehensive detection.
